spans.text: Real-world numbers tell the story: on a 2% packet loss link (common on mobile), HTTP/2 throughput can drop by 50-70% compared to HTTP/3.
Akamai's real-world data shows that for users with 2%–3% packet loss, HTTP/2 can be 1.5× to 2× slower than HTTP/1.1 (which uses multiple TCP connections, so only one connection starves).

5% packet loss scenario (loading a page with 10 resources):
TCP/HTTP/2: All 10 resources stall on each loss event
QUIC/HTTP/3: Only 1 resource stalls, other 9 continue loading
Cloudflare’s measurement shows HTTP/3 holds median page-load time within 5% of baseline at 1% packet loss, versus 30%+ degradation for HTTP/2 over TCP.
With a proxy and BBR, H2’s time decreased to 10 seconds, an improvement of 90%.
while H2 with the right congestion control algorithm (CCA) can achieve performance comparable to H3, H3’s performance is more robust
H3 excels under high-loss and high-latency conditions, leveraging connection migration and multiplexing to deliver up to 88.36% improvement in migration scenarios and 81.5% in extreme loss cases.

Our results demonstrate H3’s ability to maintain low request time and ensure seamless user experience during network transitions, highlighting its suitability for mobile and dynamic networking environments.

claims.text: On mobile networks with 2% packet loss (typical for cellular), HTTP/2 throughput drops 50-70% compared to HTTP/3; Akamai's production data shows HTTP/2 can run 1.5-2x slower than HTTP/1.1 under similar conditions. This means protocol choice should reflect expected network quality, not assume newer releases are universally faster.

meta.capability: Stop automatically upgrading to the latest protocol version and start selecting between HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 based on packet loss characteristics of your user network.

claims.text: At 5% packet loss across a 10-resource page load, TCP/HTTP/2 stalls all 10 resources on each loss event, while QUIC/HTTP/3 stalls only the 1 affected resource. Identical packet loss produces completely different observable latency signatures per protocol: HTTP/2 creates correlated stalls across all resources, while HTTP/3 creates independent per-stream delays.

meta.query: Why does packet loss result in different latency patterns between HTTP/3 and HTTP/2, and what is the technical sequence of how each handles lost packets?
meta.capability: Interpret latency spikes differently by protocol, recognizing that TCP-level stalls block all concurrent requests while QUIC-level stalls isolate to individual streams.

claims.text: Cloudflare's measurements show HTTP/3 maintains page-load time within 5% of baseline at 1% packet loss, while HTTP/2 degrades by 30%+. LAN staging environments with zero packet loss show minimal protocol differences, but production mobile networks reveal fundamental differences because packet loss exposes each protocol's distinct recovery mechanism.

claims.text: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 showed equivalent performance in laboratory tests under ideal conditions (10 Mbps, 0% loss, 0 ms delay, approximately 9 seconds for 10 MB downloads), but HTTP/3 delivered substantially faster performance in degraded conditions: with 4% packet loss and 50 ms latency, HTTP/3 completed downloads in 15 seconds while HTTP/2 required 106 seconds. This suggests operators can defer HTTP/3 investment in low-loss, low-latency network segments while prioritizing it for mobile users and geographic regions experiencing higher packet loss and latency.

claims.text: When HTTP/2 connections were routed through proxies implementing the BBR congestion control algorithm under severe impairments (4% packet loss, 50 ms latency), performance improved from 106 seconds to 10 seconds—a 90% gain that matched HTTP/3's 15-second performance. This configuration change on existing proxy infrastructure allows operators to preserve HTTP/2 deployments while achieving HTTP/3-equivalent performance in high-impairment segments.

claims.text: HTTP/3's connection migration—maintaining session continuity when clients switch between Wi-Fi and cellular networks—delivered 88.36% performance improvement in controlled testing using connection identity independent of IP address. Across all testbed scenarios evaluated for HTTP/2 (single-stream, multi-stream, proxy-enhanced), research contains no measurements demonstrating comparable session continuity during network transitions, indicating HTTP/2's IP-based TCP connection model cannot replicate this capability. For mobile operators, this segment represents a capability requirement rather than a performance optimization.
